title: Pointers in C
misconceptions: A pointer variable stores the actual value of another variable directly rather than its memory address.
Adding 1 to a pointer always increments the numerical address by exactly 1 byte regardless of the data type.
Uninitialized pointers automatically default to pointing to NULL or a safe memory address.
Array names and pointer variables are identical in all contexts, allowing array names to be reassigned to new addresses.
Dereferencing a pointer (*p) yields the address of the pointer itself.

rubric.text: Explains that a pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable rather than a standard data value.
Demonstrates how the address-of operator (&) is used to obtain the memory address of a variable.
Explains how the dereference operator (*) accesses or modifies the value stored at the memory address held by a pointer.
Clarifies that a pointer's declared type determines the type of data it points to and governs how dereferencing and arithmetic behave.
Explains the purpose of a NULL pointer as a sentinel value indicating that the pointer does not point to a valid memory location.
Explains how pointers enable pass-by-reference behavior in C functions, allowing a called function to modify the caller's variables.
Describes pointer arithmetic, specifically that adding or subtracting an integer scales the memory address by the size of the pointed-to data type.
Explains the relationship between arrays and pointers, including how array names decay into pointers to their first elements in most expressions.
Explains how pointers are used with dynamic memory allocation functions (such as malloc and free) to manage heap memory.
